extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and graduate students/researchers interested in mathematical practice and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria and methodological standards for what counts as adequate philosophy of mathematics and for assessing mathematical practice (e.g., justification of axioms, role of visualization, purity, explanation, computer proofs). Targets the subfield of philosophy of mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy of 'real' mathematics (Corfield)
rubrics_metrics.description: What then is a philosophy of real mathematics? The intention of this term is to draw a line between work informed by the concerns of mathematicians past and present and that done on the basis of at best token contact with its history or practice. (Corfield, 2003, p. 3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical work should be informed by the actual concerns, history, and practice of mathematicians; avoid purely abstract or foundationalist projects that ignore mainstream mathematical activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'foundationalist filter'
rubrics_metrics.description: By far the larger part of activity in what goes by the name philosophy of mathematics is dead to what mathematicians think and have thought, aside from an unbalanced interest in the ‘foundational’ ideas of the 1880–1930 period, yielding too often a distorted picture of that time. (Corfield, 2003, p. 5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of focusing narrowly on historical foundational debates; recommendation to broaden scope beyond early-20th-century foundations and not let that filter impoverish philosophical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should attend to actual mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophy of mathematics should concern itself with what leading mathematicians of their day have achieved, how their styles of reasoning evolve, how they justify the course along which they steer their programmes, what constitute obstacles to their programmes, how they come to view a domain as worthy of study and how their ideas shape and are shaped by the concerns of physicists and other scientists. (p. 10)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess philosophical accounts by whether they examine achievements, evolving reasoning styles, justificatory strategies, obstacles, domain-selection, and interaction with other sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why some mathematical entities are important, natural, and fruitful
rubrics_metrics.description: Why are some mathematical entities important, natural, and fruitful while others are not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory account should explain criteria by which mathematicians judge an entity's importance or fruitfulness (e.g., unifying power, generation of new results, conceptual clarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for the connectivity of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: What accounts for the connectivity of mathematics? How is it that concepts developed in one part of mathematics suddenly turn out to be connected to apparently unrelated concepts in other areas?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical accounts should address explanations for unexpected interconnections (e.g., structural explanations, conceptual unification, analogical transfer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the epistemic limits of computer proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Why are computer proofs unable to provide the sort of understanding at which mathematicians aim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the epistemic role of computer-assisted proofs: their confirmatory value, limits for understanding, and how they fit into mathematicians' explanatory standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of analogy and inductive reasoning in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the role of analogy and other types of inductive reasoning in mathematics? Can Bayesianism be applied to mathematics?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical methodology should analyze analogical and inductive forms of mathematical reasoning and assess proposals (e.g., Bayesian accounts) for capturing their justificatory strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between diagrammatic thinking and formal reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the relationship between diagrammatic thinking and formal reasoning? How to account for the fruitfulness of diagrammatic reasoning in algebraic topology?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how diagrammatic methods contribute to discovery and justification, when they are reliable, and how they relate to formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness to mathematical practice as criterion of adequacy (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithfulness to mathematical practice is for Maddy a criterion of adequacy for a satisfactory philosophy of mathematics (Maddy, 1990, p. 23 and p. 28).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical accounts should be judged by how well they conform to and explain actual mathematical practice rather than by abstract prior philosophical commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable consequence as a methodological virtue (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological considerations include: verifiable consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating theories or axioms, prefer those that yield verifiable consequences within the mathematical practice relevant to practitioners' goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful new methods as a methodological virtue (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological considerations include: powerful new methods for solving pre-existing problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value theories or axioms that enable genuinely new problem-solving techniques or methods that address previously intractable problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplifying and systematizing theories (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological considerations include: simplifying and systematizing theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess theories by their capacity to simplify mathematical practice and systematize disparate results into coherent frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implying previous conjectures as a virtue (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological considerations include: implying previous conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories that entail previously conjectured results gain support because they explain known expectations within a domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implying 'natural' results (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological considerations include: implying ‘natural’ results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for proposals that yield results considered 'natural' by practitioners (i.e., results that fit established mathematical patterns or intuitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong intertheoretic connections as a methodological virtue (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological considerations include: strong intertheoretic connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor axioms/theories that create robust links between previously separate areas, increasing explanatory reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing new insights into old theorems (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological considerations include: providing new insights into old theorem[s].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals by their ability to shed new light on established results, revealing deeper structure or simplifying their understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize and unify as guiding maxims (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maddy distills several methodological principles, such as maximize and unify, that in her final analysis direct the practice of set theorists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging axioms or theories, consider their power to maximize explanatory reach and unify disparate results and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of reliability of non-demonstrative arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: What's needed is not just a description of non-demonstrative arguments, but an account of why and when they are reliable, an account that should help set theorists make a rational choice between competing axiom candidates. (Maddy, 1990, p. 148)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical work should supply criteria to assess the reliability of inductive, heuristic, or non-deductive arguments used in mathematical theory-choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism principle: philosophy must yield to successful practice (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: If our philosophical account of mathematics comes into conflict with successful mathematical practice, it is the philosophy that must give. (Maddy, 1997, p.161)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical doctrines should be revised when they conflict with well-established, successful mathematical methods and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a naturalized model of practice (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The naturalist claims that the model accurately reflects the underlying justificatory structure of the practice: that the material excised is truly irrelevant, that the goals identified are among the actual goals of the practice (and that the various goals interact as portrayed), and that the means-ends reasoning employed is sound. (Maddy, 1997, p. 197)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A naturalized model should be evaluated by checking: (a) irrelevant philosophical material has been excised legitimately, (b) identified goals match practitioners' goals, (c) interactions among goals are represented correctly, and (d) means-ends inferences are sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical explanation as an epistemic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation is among the most important virtues that mathematicians seek. Very often the proof of a mathematical result convinces us that the result is true but does not tell us why it is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proofs and theories for their explanatory power: alternative proofs are valuable when they provide understanding, not merely demonstration of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of methods as an epistemic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of purity has played an important role in the history of mathematics... That purity is often cherished in mathematical practice is made obvious by the fact that Erdös and Selberg were awarded the Fields Medal for the elementary proof of the prime number theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether methods avoid 'ideal' elements, whether elimination of such elements yields epistemic gains, and the dialectic between purity and impurity in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness and naturalness of concepts as evaluative standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians seem to have a very good sense of when a particular mathematical concept or theory is fruitful or ‘natural’. A certain concept might provide the ‘natural’ setting for an entire development and reveal this by its fruitfulness in unifying a wide group of results or by opening unexpected new vistas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine objective features (e.g., unifying power, opening new directions) that justify judgments of naturalness and fruitfulness rather than treating them as mere subjective taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing mathematical evidence and understanding in light of computers
rubrics_metrics.description: Computers provide an aid to mathematical discovery; they provide experimental, inductive confirmation of mathematical hypotheses; they carry out calculations that are needed in proofs; and they enable one to obtain formal verification of proofs. ... calls for an extension of ordinary epistemology of mathematics that will address issues that the use of computers in mathematics make urgent, such as the problem of characterizing mathematical evidence and mathematical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical accounts should develop criteria for what counts as mathematical evidence and understanding when computer-assisted or formally verified methods are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take non-rigorous but fruitful physical arguments seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: What seemed like an inevitable divorce between physics and pure mathematics turned into an exciting renewal of vows... However, the standards of acceptability between the two disciplines are very different. ... several examples of ‘non-rigorous’ proofs in mathematics and physics are discussed with the suggestion that logicians and mathematicians should not dismiss these developments but rather try to make sense of these unruly parts of the mathematical universe and to bring the physicists’ insights into the realm of rigorous argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate influential but non-rigorous arguments by investigating how they generate fruitful conjectures, heuristic insight, or new mathematics, and seek ways to render their insights rigorous where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend analytic philosophy tools to neglected topics
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not dismiss the analytic tradition in philosophy of mathematics but rather seek to extend its tools to a variety of areas that have been, by and large, ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply analytic methods (e.g., conceptual analysis, models of explanation) to localized case studies like visualization, diagrammatic reasoning, purity, category theory, and mathematical physics to evaluate practice.
